title: AI in Education #1: Five Things I Learned from Daisy Christodoulou
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton distills five takeaways from a conversation with Daisy Christodoulou of No More Marking, whose team dismissed AI as a decade away from useful just three weeks before ChatGPT launched. Christodoulou warns that impressive agreement statistics can mask a model that has simply found a shortcut -- an early 1968 essay marker scored well because it was really just measuring essay length -- so she insists on qualitative review of AI/human disagreements rather than headline agreement rates. Counter-intuitively, AI performs better at comparative judgement (which of two essays is better) than absolute judgement (assign a rubric score), and when her team traced 400,000 human/AI disagreements, nearly all turned out to be human error, often handwriting bias. She argues humans must stay in the loop -- to catch what we don't yet understand about the models, to deter gaming, and because junior professionals need the 'grunt work' of marking to develop expertise -- landing on a 10% human / 90% AI split. Personalised AI tutors still face three unsolved problems: explanations alone don't teach, hallucination rates well above zero compound at national scale, and screen time in the primary years. Her closing principle, and the one Barton returns to, is to always start with the problem being solved rather than what the technology can do.
points: A model's headline agreement rate can hide a shortcut it has learned to game -- the 1968 essay marker scored well because it was effectively marking on length, a caution against evaluating AI tools by agreement percentage alone.

AI performs more reliably on comparative judgement (which piece is better) than absolute judgement (assign a rubric score), and in a 400,000-essay audit nearly all human/AI disagreements traced back to human error, especially handwriting bias.

No More Marking deliberately keeps 10% human judgement in the loop -- not because the AI is worse, but to catch model blind spots, deter student gaming, and preserve the 'grunt work' that turns junior markers into experts.

Even a well-tuned AI tutor's 0.14% hallucination rate becomes roughly a million errors a year if scaled to every student in Britain, which is why Christodoulou resists framing AI tutors as a finished, error-free product.

Her operating principle for any school AI decision is to ask 'what problem does this solve?' rather than 'what can this do?' -- the same test she applies to her own product roadmap at No More Marking.
quotes: We were like, you know, it's still not there. There's nothing there that's really going to help us.

I would rather a model that had 80% agreement and wasn't marking on length than one that had 95% and was marking on length, because that 95% one would degrade rapidly the minute people work out what it's doing.
So far, I genuinely would say all of them are the result of human error. Not AI error.
Maybe a lot of the work of junior professionals can be done very well by AI. But that grunt work is what turns you into the senior professional.
Germany has no speed limits on its motorways and car-free medieval town centres. And that is my analogy for technology in schools.
It is so easy – and I include myself in this – to get dazzled by what AI can do and forget to ask whether it should.
